summary:
Consensual sex between men is a criminal offence in Kenya under the colonial-era Penal Code, carrying imprisonment of up to 14 years, and the provision is applied regardless of the nationality of those involved. No Kenyan statute governs gender identity, and there is no codified pathway for legal gender recognition; intersex people are legally recognised as a third gender, according to the UK Home Office country policy and information note of February 2025.

Legal gender recognition is obstructed in practice. Evidence before the Milimani High Court in Nairobi, in a decision delivered on 20 May 2026 by Justice Bahati Mwamuye in Petition 27 of 2020, showed that 94 per cent of trans and gender-diverse Kenyans had been refused by civil registration offices, with some applicants spending close to four years' wages on document corrections that failed. Kenya has never had a codified legal framework for gender recognition.

Courts have ordered state action. On 12 August 2025 the Eldoret High Court directed the Kenyan government to enact a Transgender Protection Rights Act, after finding that prisons fail dignity and privacy protections; the petition was brought by a trans Kenyan subjected to non-consensual medical procedures and a court-ordered 'gender determination' while incarcerated.

Police harassment is routine for trans people. Twenty-six interviewees in Mombasa and Nairobi described detention on pretexts such as being drunk and disorderly, on-the-spot extortion demands of 5,000 shillings, and the practice of using traditionally male names as pseudonyms to move through public life safely amid widespread anti-LGBTQ+ sentiment.

Violence against LGBT people is documented and sometimes lethal. In December 2024 a Kenyan man was sentenced to 50 years in jail for killing an LGBTQ activist. The Kenya Human Rights Commission's 'Lives on the Line' report of September 2025, produced with more than 14 community organisations, is the first comprehensive documentation of human-rights violations against sexual and gender minorities in Kenya, covering October 2023 to September 2024; it explicitly challenges the 2019 High Court ruling in Petition 16 of 2019 that dismissed LGBTIQ+ violence claims for purported lack of evidence.

LGBTI civil-society groups may register and operate, but only within a restrictive civic space. The Mombasa Court of Appeal ruled in 2018 that forced anal testing was unconstitutional, with compensation awarded in 2024, and the Supreme Court upheld freedom of association in 2023, allowing LGBTQ organisation registration; a petition against incitement to hatred and discrimination remains before the courts. Societal discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation is widespread and has caused loss of employment and education.
tangentialFactors:
The direction of travel is court-driven rather than statutory: constitutional litigation has produced recognition of forced anal testing as unconstitutional, freedom of association for LGBTQ organisations, and a 2025 order to legislate transgender protection, while the underlying criminal provisions remain in force.

Health and research services have been targeted on religious grounds. In February 2010 religious leaders in Mtwapa demanded the closure of a KEMRI HIV research institute, an episode that bears on access to care for men who have sex with men. Documentation of discrimination against LGBT people in employment and education was already recorded by the US State Department for the 2010 reporting year, indicating that the pattern of exclusion long predates the current reporting cycle.

Kenya's framework is more developed on intersex recognition than on gender identity generally: third-gender status for intersex people sits alongside the absence of any statute governing trans identities, so visitors who are intersex and visitors who are trans face different legal positions.
localsOnly:
Kenya Human Rights Commission's 'Lives on the Line' (September 2025) draws on purposive sampling of organisations active in advocacy, data collection and service provision, and was built with more than 14 community organisations; it covers the period October 2023 to September 2024.

Active LGBTIQ+ organisations raise public awareness and provide community spaces, and operate within the Constitution's Article 28 guarantee of dignity, even as the report's data record violence against their communities.

Residents may register and run LGBTI organisations following the Supreme Court's 2023 affirmation of freedom of association, and a petition against incitement to hatred and discrimination has been filed by advocates.

The Eldoret High Court's 12 August 2025 judgment obliges the state to legislate a Transgender Protection Rights Act and to remedy prison conditions that fail dignity and privacy for trans detainees.
outOfScopeNotes:
Enforcement data on prosecutions under the Penal Code's same-sex conduct provision are not sourced in this inventory; the record establishes the offence and its maximum penalty, not how often it is used against visitors or residents.

Whether the Transgender Protection Rights Act directed by the Eldoret High Court on 12 August 2025 has been enacted, and in what form, is unresolved here.

The practical effect of the Milimani High Court's 20 May 2026 decision on civil registration offices, including whether refusals of document corrections have declined, is not sourced.

The scope of intersex third-gender recognition in practice, including which documents carry the marker and whether it extends to non-intersex trans people, is not established by these sources.

Only the killing of an LGBTQ activist and the resulting 50-year sentence are documented; broader patterns of anti-trans homicide with dates and outcomes are not itemised in this inventory.
